source.title_on_document: Human-AI Co-Creativity: Does ChatGPT Make Us More Creative?

supplement.where: None referenced. The paper cites no supplementary material, online appendix, or supporting information. Its end matter (p. 9) is Acknowledgments, Ethics Statement, Conflicts of Interest, Data Availability Statement ('Data available on request.'), and References.
supplement.holds: Nothing outside this PDF. Per-arm analyzed counts for the DAT and pairwise Tukey HSD statistics or p-values are printed nowhere. The paper gives allocation counts (Table 1, p. 4), arm means and SDs (p. 6), and the omnibus F (p. 6).

paper_design_summary: Students at an urban university in the US Midwest were randomly allocated to one of six priming conditions in a 2 (prime source label: 'a student' vs 'ChatGPT') x 3 (prime creativity: low, typical, high) between-subjects design. Each participant saw one seven-noun example answer to the Divergent Association Task (DAT), retyped it, rated how creative it was, and then completed the DAT themselves. At each level the list was identical under both labels, the Methods do not say who produced the lists, and no participant used an AI tool. The paper's 387 participants are the people retained after an end-of-study attention check (see exclusions), and 381 were analyzed on the DAT. The scored output is each participant's own DAT score (semantic distance among the participant's own words).

studies.label: 2 x 3 priming experiment (prime source label x prime creativity level), Divergent Association Task

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of six priming conditions: an example DAT response (seven nouns) of low, typical, or high creativity, presented as coming from 'a student' or from 'ChatGPT'. Participants were not told the creativity level. At each level the list was identical under both labels, so the source factor varies only the attributed source. The arms' ai codes record the stated source. Because both arms at a level received the same list, one of the two codes misdescribes the list's origin, which the Methods do not state (open question 2).
assignment.quote: Participants responded to a set of demographic questions and a suite of personality, creativity, and AI covariates before being randomly allocated to one of six priming conditions.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1 Design and Participants; p. 4, Section 3.2 Procedure and Section 3.3 Priming; p. 4, Table 1

participants.exclusions: The attention check came at the end of the study, after allocation (p. 4, Section 3.4 and Figure 1), and participants who failed it 'were removed from the sample'. The paper does not say how many failed. The 387 that the paper gives as the result of random allocation (p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 4, Table 1) are the people kept after that removal: all 387 enter the perceived-creativity ANOVA, F (5, 381) (p. 6, Section 4.2), and Table 3 gives prime creativity N = 387 (p. 5). So n_randomized (387) and the arm counts (Table 1) are counts of people allocated and retained. They equal the number randomized only if no one failed the check. DAT score N = 381 (Table 3, p. 5), consistent with the DAT ANOVA's F (5, 375) (p. 6), so 381 were analyzed on the DAT. The 6 missing DAT scores are not explained, and per-arm DAT counts are not printed. Table 3 lists 'Total (valid)' N = 376, while the hierarchical regression's degrees of freedom (F (1, 376) at step 1, F(6, 371) at step 5) correspond to 378 observations.
participants.who: Students at an urban university in the Midwest of the United States ('a university student sample', p. 8): 107 male, 273 female, 6 non-binary, fluid, or transgender, 1 declined; 68.99 percent white or Caucasian; mean age 23.87.
participants.quote: Participants (N = 387), drawn from an urban university in the Midwest of the United States, took part in a study using a 2 (Prime Source: Human vs. ChatGPT) x 3 (Prime Creativity: Low, Typical, High) factorial design.

ai_tool.name_model: Labeled 'ChatGPT'; no model or version named. The paper says the lists' creativity level 'was determined from a sample (Cropley 2023) of ChatGPT responses (N = 102)' and that each list 'was selected' at a given percentile rank (p. 4). The Methods do not say who produced each list. The paper's 'ChatGPT Output' (x-axis labels of Figures 2 and 3, pp. 6-7) and 'generated by ChatGPT' (Discussion, p. 7) may follow the label, because the same figures call the identical lists 'Human Output' in the student-labeled arms (see open_questions).
ai_tool.how_used: No participant used an AI tool. Each participant saw one example DAT response (seven nouns) presented as from 'a student' or from 'ChatGPT', retyped it, rated its creativity on a 1-5 scale, and then did the DAT (p. 4, Sections 3.2 and 3.3). Percentile ranks relative to human norms: low PR = 0.05 in the text (0.03 in the Table 2 header), typical PR = 64.69 (selected to be as close as possible to the ChatGPT mean of 64.93), high PR = 95.75 (p. 4). Whether the list stayed on screen during the DAT is not stated. The role ideas_supplied describes the ChatGPT-labeled arms as the paper presents them. It holds only if the lists are ChatGPT outputs, which the Methods do not state (open question 2).

task.description: Divergent Association Task (Olson et al. 2021): 'Please enter 10 words that are as different from each other as possible, in all meanings and uses of the words', with five rules (single English words, nouns only, no proper nouns, no specialized vocabulary, think of the words on your own) (p. 5, Section 3.5.2.2). Reported as DAT score and DAT percentile rank.

outcomes.name: DAT score (verbal divergent ideation)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Divergent Association Task (Olson et al. 2021): each participant enters 10 nouns 'as different from each other as possible'. The paper refers to 'the same underlying method (semantic distance)' (p. 5) and gives no further scoring details. Table 3 (p. 5): DAT score N = 381, min 61.16, max 94.45, mean 80.25, SD 6.30. Table 3 also lists DAT percentile rank (N = 381, mean 60.28, SD 27.59), a variant of the same score; the ANOVA means (76.37 to 82.18) are on the DAT score scale. Analyses: one-way between-groups ANOVA over the six conditions with Tukey HSD post hoc tests (H1, Section 4.1, p. 6); hierarchical regression (H3, Section 4.3, p. 6) in which 'priming condition' enters at step 5 with 1 df: model 8.7% of variance, F(6, 371) = 5.90, p < 0.001; R squared change = 0.000, F change (1, 371) = 0.05, p = 0.824. That step is a model comparison, not a two-arm contrast. Construct coded flexibility under the codebook rule 'Variety among one person's own ideas is flexibility': the score measures how far apart one participant's own words are, and the paper calls divergent thinking 'only one facet of creativity' (p. 8, Section 6.1). The codebook's table defines flexibility as a count of categories, which the DAT is not, and other forms code the DAT as other (c069, c158) or flexibility (c126), so Review 1 should set one code for the DAT (open question 6). ai_available_when_produced coded no and question after_ai: the paper describes the prime, its retyping, and its rating as steps completed before the DAT ('Lastly, participants completed the DAT themselves', p. 4, Section 3.2; Figure 1), and it never says the list stayed on screen. Review 1 may prefer with_ai, because the paper treats the prime as 'assistance given' for the DAT (Hypothesis 1, p. 3) and the AI exposure before the DAT was one short look at a seven-noun list (open question 3). The two level contrasts are coded ai_design on the paper's framing of level as 'the level of creativity of that assistance' (p. 3, Section 2.2). The paper does not call the levels AI configurations or the typical list a default, and the code holds only if the lists are ChatGPT outputs (open question 2). Otherwise those pairs vary an example's content under a shared ChatGPT label and would be coded other.

eligibility.reason: Criteria 2 and 3 are met. Individuals were randomly allocated to six priming conditions (p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 4, Section 3.2), and 381 were analyzed on the DAT (Table 3, p. 5; F (5, 375), p. 6), far above 50. The DAT score is an automated semantic-distance score of each participant's own list of 10 nouns. Criterion 1 is unclear. No participant used an AI tool. Each saw one seven-noun example, told it came from 'a student' or from 'ChatGPT', and at each creativity level the list was identical under both labels. The three source contrasts therefore vary only the stated source, not AI assistance, and do not meet criterion 1. Criterion 1 rests on the two level contrasts among ChatGPT-labeled arms (ChLo vs ChTy, ChHi vs ChTy), which vary the example's content. They count only if the lists are ChatGPT outputs, which the Methods do not state (the low list's percentile rank lies below the GPT-4 range that the paper reports for Cropley 2023, p. 2), and only if Review 1 treats a one-shot example of a different creativity level as a different AI configuration.

one_line_finding: Mean DAT score was 76.37 (SD 5.71) after the low-creativity example presented as from ChatGPT versus 79.74 to 82.18 in the other five conditions, including 79.96 (SD 5.94) for the same list presented as from a student (F (5, 375) = 6.39, p < 0.001, eta squared = 0.08; Tukey HSD: only ChLo differed; p. 6, Section 4.1, Figure 2).
open_questions: Criterion 1 rests on the two level contrasts among ChatGPT-labeled arms (ChLo vs ChTy, ChHi vs ChTy). Review 1 should decide whether a one-shot example of a different creativity level, presented as ChatGPT output, counts as a different AI configuration (ai_design). The three source-label contrasts do not meet criterion 1, because each pair received the identical list and differed only in the stated source. They stay coded other.

Who produced each prime list is not stated in the Methods. The text says the creativity level 'was determined from a sample (Cropley 2023) of ChatGPT responses (N = 102)' and that each list 'was selected' at a percentile rank (p. 4). The Discussion calls the ChLo prime 'a low-creativity list of words generated by ChatGPT' (p. 7), but Figures 2 and 3 label the identical lists 'Human Output' in the student-labeled arms and 'ChatGPT Output' in the ChatGPT-labeled arms (pp. 6-7), so the paper's output wording follows the label. The low list's PR (0.05 in the text, 0.03 in Table 2) lies below the 31.03 to 99.60 range that the paper reports for GPT-4 in Cropley (2023) (p. 2). If all three lists are ChatGPT outputs, the student-labeled arms also saw ChatGPT text. If the low list is not, ChLo received no AI output, and the ChLo vs ChTy contrast does not compare two AI outputs.

Whether the prime stayed on screen during the DAT is not stated. The form codes ai_available_when_produced no and question after_ai, because the paper describes the prime and its rating as steps completed before the DAT, which participants 'completed ... themselves' (p. 4, Section 3.2; Figure 1). Review 1 may prefer with_ai, because the paper treats the prime as 'assistance given' for the DAT (Hypothesis 1, p. 3) and the AI exposure was one short look at a seven-noun list.
Setting not stated (supervised session or online). design_class is kept as lab_rct.

The number removed by the attention check is not stated, so the 387 retained equal the number randomized only if no one failed. Per-arm DAT counts are not printed (381 analyzed on the DAT of the 387 retained), and the 6 missing DAT scores are not explained.

Construct: the DAT score is coded flexibility under the codebook rule 'Variety among one person's own ideas is flexibility', but the codebook's table defines flexibility as a count of categories. Other forms code the DAT as other (c069, c158) or flexibility (c126). Review 1 should set one code for the DAT.
notes: Inconsistencies: the low-creativity prime's PR is 0.05 in the text (p. 4, Section 3.3) and 0.03 in the Table 2 header (p. 4); Table 3 'Total (valid)' N = 376, while the regression degrees of freedom correspond to 378 observations (p. 6). Not listed as an outcome, because it is a rating of the prime and not of the participant's own output (form-spec rule 7): perceived creativity of the prime, 1-5 scale; F (5, 381) = 71.90, p < 0.001, eta squared = 0.48; HuLo M = 1.91, SD = 0.98; ChLo M = 2.04, SD = 1.14; HuTy M = 4.16, SD = 0.85; HuHi M = 4.13, SD = 0.80; ChTy M = 3.73, SD = 1.01; ChHi M = 3.93, SD = 0.94; Tukey HSD: HuLo and ChLo differ from the other four (p. 6, Section 4.2; Figure 3, p. 7). Contrasts not listed: pairs of human-labeled levels (no AI-labeled arm) and ChHi vs ChLo (neither arm is the typical list, which the form uses as the control). Tukey HSD found ChLo different from every other condition, ChHi included, and the paper calls the other five conditions 'statistically indistinguishable' (p. 7). The hierarchical regression (H3) is in measure_detail; its step 4 adds perceived prime creativity (R squared change = 0.029, F change (1, 372) = 11.81, p < 0.001; p. 6). Construct coded flexibility (measure_detail and open question 6). The reconciled form had overall_creativity, because the paper uses the DAT as its creativity measure (H1, p. 3). statistics_available lists only arm_means_sds_ns: the only DAT test across arms is the six-group omnibus F, which tests no single pair, the Tukey HSD results are given only in words, and the ns are Table 1 counts of people allocated and retained, not per-arm analyzed counts. Figures 2 and 3 print two error-bar labels, 'Error Bars: 95% CI' and 'Error Bars: +/- 2 SE' (pp. 6-7). Covariates measured before allocation: openness (BFI-2), creative self-efficacy, propensity to trust AI, creative personal identity, AI familiarity. Ethics: University of Nebraska at Omaha IRB, Application 0223-23-EX (p. 9).

challenge_resolution.problem: Criterion 1: the source factor randomizes a belief about who produced the same list, not AI assistance, so the three source contrasts fail criterion 1 and only the level contrasts can meet it. The form had left the source contrasts to Review 1 as possible ai_vs_active contrasts.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: eligibility.reason now says the three source contrasts (ChLo vs HuLo, ChTy vs HuTy, ChHi vs HuHi) vary only the stated source of an identical list and do not meet criterion 1, and that criterion 1 rests on the two level contrasts among ChatGPT-labeled arms. Open question 1 no longer offers ai_vs_active for the source contrasts. It asks only whether the level contrasts count. The source contrasts stay coded other, and criterion_1 stays unclear.
challenge_resolution.quote: To test that assumption this study primed subjects with lists of words purportedly either from a human or from ChatGPT, and of varying degrees of creativity.
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 3, Section 2.1 (last sentence) and Hypothesis 1 ('perceived source'); p. 4, Section 3.3 Priming, second paragraph

challenge_resolution.problem: arms[].ai codes the ChatGPT-labeled arms generative_ai and the student-labeled arms other_aid, but at each level both arms received the same list, so the codes record only what participants were told, and one code in each pair misdescribes the list's origin.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Each arm description and assignment.what_was_assigned now say that the ai code records the stated source and that the paired arm received the same list. The codes stay as they were, because the label is the manipulated factor and the paper does not say which code misdescribes the material (open question 2).
challenge_resolution.quote: Thus, participants in the “low” creativity condition (regardless of source) received a unique list of nouns (Table 2);
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3 Priming, second paragraph; p. 4, Table 2 (three lists for six arms)

challenge_resolution.problem: ai_tool.role ideas_supplied presumes AI-generated examples, but the Methods never say who produced the lists, the low list's percentile rank lies below the GPT-4 range the paper reports for Cropley (2023), and the paper's 'ChatGPT Output' wording follows the label.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: ai_tool.role stays ideas_supplied, which describes the ChatGPT-labeled arms as the paper presents them. ai_tool.name_model, ai_tool.how_used, and open question 2 now add the checker's evidence: Figures 2 and 3 label the identical lists 'Human Output' or 'ChatGPT Output' by arm, so the paper's output wording, and possibly the Discussion's 'generated by ChatGPT', follow the label. If the lists are not ChatGPT outputs, the role would be other. Only the authors can say who produced each list.
challenge_resolution.quote: The creativity level of the list of nouns was determined from a sample (Cropley 2023) of ChatGPT responses (N = 102) with a mean Percentile Rank (relative to human norms) of 64.93 (SD = 21.75).
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3 Priming and Table 2 header; p. 2, left column, first paragraph (GPT-4 range 31.03 to 99.60); p. 6, Figure 2 x-axis labels; p. 7, Figure 3 x-axis labels and Discussion, second paragraph

challenge_resolution.problem: The level contrasts (ChLo vs ChTy, ChHi vs ChTy) are coded ai_design with ChTy as control because the typical list 'is the default configuration', but the paper never calls the typical list a default or the levels AI configurations.

It quotes the paper and says the form uses ChTy as control under the codebook's plain-or-default rule. The two control_arm entries say the paper does not call it a default. measure_detail and open questions 1 and 2 say the ai_design code rests on the paper's framing of level as 'the level of creativity of that assistance' and holds only if the lists are ChatGPT outputs. Otherwise the pairs would be coded other. comparison_type stays ai_design.
challenge_resolution.quote: Note that the typical creativity list was selected to be as close to the mean of ChatGPT responses as possible.

challenge_resolution.problem: ai_available_when_produced is yes, but the paper never says the list stayed on screen during the DAT. It describes the prime and its rating as steps before the DAT, and the DAT rules ask participants to think of the words on their own.

challenge_resolution.problem: question with_ai needs AI to be available while the DAT was written. The codebook rule gives after_ai for an outcome produced after AI is removed, and the form recorded with_ai as if it were settled.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: question changed from with_ai to after_ai, following ai_available_when_produced no and the codebook rule 'An outcome produced after AI is removed is after_ai whatever its construct.' measure_detail and open question 3 say Review 1 may prefer with_ai, because the paper treats the prime as 'assistance given' for the DAT and the AI exposure was one short look at a seven-noun list. challenge_resolution.problem: construct overall_creativity does not fit: the DAT score measures how far apart one participant's own words are, which the codebook calls flexibility, and the paper calls divergent thinking only one facet of creativity.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: construct changed from overall_creativity to flexibility under the codebook rule 'Variety among one person's own ideas is flexibility'. measure_detail, notes, and new open question 6 say that the codebook's table defines flexibility as a count of categories, which the DAT is not, and that other forms code the DAT as other (c069, c158) or flexibility (c126), so Review 1 should set one DAT code. Criterion 3 does not depend on the construct.
challenge_resolution.quote: Divergent thinking, while central to many definitions of creativity, represents only one facet of creativity.
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 8, Section 6.1 Limitations; p. 5, Section 3.5.2.2 (DAT instructions and 'the same underlying method (semantic distance)'); codebook section 6, Construct

Whether the prime stayed on screen during the DAT, which decides between after_ai (now coded) and with_ai (open question 3). If it did not, Review 1 may still prefer with_ai for a one-shot example shown just before the task.
